title: Master Class | Sicilian Defence, Smith–Morra Gambit | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Take the pawn — and it looks like a Smith-Morra is coming.
Yes, the Smith-Morra. I don't recommend accepting it — for people who don't want to get mated, there are clean ways to decline.
The best decline I've found without taking the pawn is the knight to f6 — you develop and counterattack the e4-pawn, and White essentially has to transpose with e5.
He plays the bishop to d3 rather than e5.
Now we take the pawn — a much better version of the Morra, because with the bishop on d3 instead of c4 it just stares at its own pawn, and White's activity is muted.
e5 would weaken the d5 square — he could pin with the bishop to g5, trade the knight, and plant a piece there. Instead, the flexible knight to c6, and then d6.
d6, to stop him playing e5.
In the Morra his bishop usually sits on c4, which changes everything — here we can breathe. h3 is a good move, stopping our bishop from coming to g4.
There's no urgency to our development, so g6 and the bishop to g7 — since e5 isn't possible, we can afford to give the bishop its best square.
The bishop to g5 doesn't threaten the knight, so we needn't move it — the question is whether to play h6.
Play h6 first, while the rook is still home: his plan is Qd2 and the bishop to h6, trading off our dark-squared bishop — our strongest piece, whose loss would leave the kingside full of holes.
Now castle, playing it conventionally.
The king to h7 — the key move; it supports the pawn, and without it the whole h6 idea falls apart.
The king is quite safe on h7 — the pawn guards against the check and the chain holds; just keep an eye on the pin down the road.
We don't play e5 — it would blunt our bishop and still weaken d5.
Address the bishop instead — out to e6. Normally a square to avoid, but here it's a fine post: centralised, controlling d5, and we don't need the e-pawn for now.
The rook to c8, activating and contesting the c-file — not every move has to climb Everest; solid improving moves keep the edge.
The knight to d7 is lovely: it can reroute to e5 or c5, it covers the d4 square, and it opens the bishop's diagonal.
The knight to e5 — the secondary point behind d7. It isn't really blocking the bishop again, because this knight won't stay: it either takes his important bishop or hops into c4.
The knight to c5, and if he shifts the bishop away, the knight to c4 is very strong. The a7-pawn is offered deliberately — losing it wouldn't be the end of the world, and White is stuck either way.
White's best is to give up the bishop with Bd4 — thinking ahead so it doesn't lose all its effectiveness in the coming trade.
Take with the bishop — the positionally conscious choice; recapturing with the queen would allow the rook to c1 with tempo on the file.
The knight to c4 — and the bishop to c2 was an inaccuracy, even a mistake; White's position here is simply worse.

Here's the idea some forget: a vulnerable queen can be 'attacked' by your own queen to force a trade — welcome when you're up a pawn or want a file. We hit the bishop, hit the queen, force the trade, stay a pawn up, and dominate the queenside.
